title: Song pluggers, Nick Clesi and playing for house dances
summary: Talk of local song pluggers; she says music was rare then and she played for dances in private homes.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: I have a book on the rise of sports in New Orleans.

I'll try to look it up. When I listen to this, I'll remember to do it. But it covers the early days of sports. I guess I knew a couple of people that plugged songs. It seemed to me Sammy Rosenbaum did. Sam Rosenbaum. He worked for Triangle. Maybe he managed it. It was Treasurer or something. That's a local firm.
No, I didn't know. I didn't know.
Well, he and Classy, who wrote, I'm sorry I made you cry.
Yeah, they were all tied in together. Rosenbaum and Joe Virgis and Erwin LeClerc. But you knew Classy, Nick Classy then.

I knew Mr. Classy. I knew him personally. I remember what he looked like. But, well, music, of course, in those days. Honey, you didn't have a television. You didn't have a radio. You didn't have music under your nose all the time. You know what I mean? Yeah. The only time you heard any music was when you went to a show or down to the store and asked somebody to play some pieces for you. And then you, what did I start to say about the dances? You know, I played for dances at first. Just in somebody's residence. They'd have somebody with a big home. I can remember going up off on Napoleon Avenue up there. And just playing the piano and the young people all dancing. It wasn't like a bigger function or anything. No. It'd just be groups that got together. But the number of people who could play were scarce, really.
